title: Directed Writing
tagline: Writing prose pieces to a given brief: reports, speeches, articles, proposals and formal and informal letters.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material and original practice questions written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI English Language (Paper 1) syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus topic was taken from the official-verified ISC English registry entry; no CISCE examination paper was consulted, so every example and every practice question is original and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Directed writing asks you to write in a particular form, for a particular reader, and to a particular purpose. Unlike a free composition, the task is partly set for you: you must shape what you say to fit the brief. In ISC English, directed writing includes letters, speeches, reports, articles, proposals and related prose forms. The key skills are reading the question carefully, choosing a suitable tone and approach, and organising the response so that it is clear, complete and not merely a collection of good sentences.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Reading the brief; choosing the right form, tone and register; audience awareness; completeness; structure; following instructions in the prompt

learningOutcomes: Interpret a directed writing task accurately.
Choose a suitable form, tone and register.
Include the points required by the question.
Write for a specific reader rather than for a vague audience.
Check that the final piece matches the brief.

blocks.text: The first step in directed writing is not writing at all; it is reading the question with care. Directed writing tasks usually tell you what to say, who you are writing to, and why. Some tasks also give you a set of notes or prompts to use. If you miss a required point, the writing may sound competent but incomplete. Before starting, identify the form, the audience, the purpose and the points that must be covered.

items: Identify the form of writing required.
Mark any points that you must include.
Note any tone, style or length clues in the question.

items.text: If the task says 'Write a letter to the editor suggesting one change to improve traffic in your town', the reader is the editor and the public, the purpose is to propose and justify a single change, and the letter should not drift into unrelated complaints.
items.note: A clear brief makes the response easier to control.

blocks.text: Directed writing is a good test of register: the style appropriate to the situation. A letter to a school principal asks for a different tone from a letter to a friend. A speech to a school assembly should be engaging and appropriate to a listening audience. A report to a committee should be formal and objective. Register is not just about being formal or informal; it is about choosing the level of seriousness, the degree of objectivity, and the kind of language that fits the reader and the purpose.

items: A formal letter should be polite, measured and purposeful.
An informal letter may be warmer and more conversational, while still being correct.
A speech should suit a listening audience; it can be more direct and lively.
A report should be clear, factual and well organised.
An article should interest a general reader without losing accuracy.

items.text: In a formal complaint letter, 'I wish to bring to your attention a serious problem with the library timetable' is more suitable than a blunt, casual complaint. In a letter to a friend, that same tone would sound odd and distant.
items.note: The same facts can be phrased very differently depending on the audience.

blocks.text: Some directed writing tasks are prose forms that may feel unfamiliar if you have written mainly letters. An article is written for a magazine or newspaper reader; it should engage the reader, develop a clear main idea, and often has a title or heading. A report is usually written for a specific person or group and should be organised under clear points or sections. A speech is meant to be spoken, so it should be direct, with a clear opening, connected points, and a closing that fits the occasion. Each form has its own conventions, but in every case the task's brief comes first.

items: An article should interest a reader and develop one main idea.
A report should be organised, factual and addressed to the right person or group.
A speech should be written for the ear, with a clear opening and ending.
A proposal should explain the suggestion and why it is worth carrying out.
Every form still needs a clear response to the prompt.

items.text: If asked to write a report on a school event for the principal, the report should not read like a speech to the event audience; it should give a clear account, with relevant observations, for someone who was not there.
items.note: The form shapes the wording even when the content is similar.

keyPoints: Directed writing is controlled by the brief, not by the writer's preference.
Always identify form, audience and purpose before writing.
Register matters: the tone should suit the reader.
Include all the points the question asks for.
Organise the response so it is easy to follow.
examFocus: Most marks in directed writing are lost when a student writes something plausible but does not answer the exact task.
A brief, well-organised response that follows the instructions is usually better than a longer one that wanders.

vocabulary.meaning: Writing that follows a specific brief in form, audience and purpose.
The style and tone suitable for a particular reader, purpose and situation.
The reader or listener the writing is aimed at.
The instructions and requirements of the task.
A formal written account of an activity, event or issue, usually for a specific reader.
A spoken address meant to be heard, with an opening, a development and a conclusion that suits the occasion.

questions.prompt: In directed writing, the first thing to do before writing is to:
options: Read the brief carefully and note the form, audience and required points
Ignore the prompt and write a general essay
questions.answer: Read the brief carefully and note the form, audience and required points
questions.explanation: Directed writing depends on answering the specific task, so the brief matters more than the writer's preference.
questions.commonMistake: Beginning to write before checking what the question actually asks.

questions.prompt: A speech is best written to suit:
questions.explanation: A speech is meant to be heard, so it should be written for the ear and the occasion.
questions.commonMistake: Writing a speech as if it were a formal report or a private note.

questions.prompt: Why is register important in directed writing? Give one example.
questions.answer: Register matters because the same task may require different tones for different readers. For example, a letter to the principal should be polite and formal, while a letter to a friend can be more informal and personal.
questions.explanation: Register is the match between language and situation.
questions.commonMistake: Treating every task as if it required the same tone.

questions.prompt: State two features of a good report.
questions.answer: A good report is organised, usually with clear points; it is addressed to the correct reader; and it gives relevant information and observations in a factual, readable way.
questions.explanation: Reports are practical documents, so clarity and organisation matter.
questions.commonMistake: Saying a report is just a long complaint without structure.

questions.prompt: You have been asked to write a proposal to the head teacher suggesting one improvement to the school library. List the points you would make and the order you would use them in.
questions.answer: Likely points: first, state the current problem; second, suggest a specific improvement; third, explain why it would help; fourth, say who would be responsible or how it might be carried out; fifth, conclude with the benefit. The order should move from problem to suggestion to benefit.
questions.explanation: A proposal should be practical and organised, not just a general wish.
questions.commonMistake: Asking for many unrelated changes without explaining why any one of them matters.
